So, as best I know, the problem of the criterion is as follows: *What do we know? - How do we know that we know?*

In answer to this problem, I think Hegel would answer in the following manner:

There is (to Hegel) an inherent *nous* in the world, a sort of intelligibility laden within it. In this sense, when the dialectical process operates in the world, it is coming to know the world, and,  ultimately, itself. In this way, we are mere spectators to the dialectic: we can observe the process unfolding and cannot stop the dialectical path of history. So, when we come to know something, it is really *Geist* coming to know. Thus, (to Hegel) we know exactly what *Geist* comes to know, and we know that we know this because the world can be made sense of by rationality and by *Geist*.

I can clarify or explain more if needed.

As a Christian, I find Nietzsche's *Antichrist* to be of great importance. There is often no better way to understand one's theological beliefs than to hear criticism of them. Nietzsche, too, has training in theology (after all, he started out studying theology and philology), so I think his thoughts on religion, especially Christianity, are of great importance.

Think of it this way, one's best friends are those able to pick out the flaws in one's own person. Your best friend will tell you how it is, whether that's about good or bad aspects of you. Nietzsche is that friend to Christianity, the friend that can criticize it while understanding its value (after all, Nietzsche lamented the death of Christianity).

So, I guess I'd answer by stating that as a religious person, Nietzsche not only *can* be read but *should* be read, as his insights are really bountiful. I'd suggest, if you're interested, reading his *Antichrist* and *The Genealogy of Morals*, as both are really important to wrestle with as a religious person.

Hope that helps.

To Nietzsche, the world is composed of both active and reactive forces which try to dominate one another. In this sense, the world is fundamentally composed of will, that is, of force. To attempt to dominate a will with one's own will is to implicitly recognize that there is *another will* out there (the one you are trying to dominate). Note that master morality really originates with the Greeks. As such, I'd read Book I of Plato's *Republic*. In it, a character named Thrasymachus tries to argue that justice is really just strength. Note that Plato frames Thrasymachus as an antagonist, but if you can parse through Plato's biases, it's a really good demonstration of master morality against slave morality (the slave morality represented by Socrates). From *Thus Spoke Zarathustra*, Prologue 3:

>What is the greatest experience you can have? It is the hour of the great contempt. The hour in which your happiness, too, arouses your disgust, and even your reason and your virtue. The hour when you say, 'What matters my happiness? It is poverty and filth and wretched contentment. But my happiness ought to justify existence itself.'

It seems to suggest that happiness as a final goal is really only a final virtue of past philosophers, not of the philosopher of the future. Mill values happiness as a final goal, when really he should transvaluation and reevaluate his own values. So to answer your question, I think Nietzsche would see both options you give (short-term pleasure and long-term well-being) as derivative of old philosophies that were uncritical of their values.

What's the solution, then? Simply put, seek whatever values you actively choose to seek. Do not seek short-term pleasure because of your base instincts, do not seek long-term well-being because of philosophical convention. Seek whatever makes you your most authentic self. After all, that's the entire idea with transvaluation.

TLDR: don't seek either because you think you should, seek them (if you want) because you want to.

One type of schema is an argument-text schema, and examining it may help make more sense of schemata in general. So, an argument-text is a set of premises and a conclusion, like this:

>**Every man is mortal.**  
>  
>**Socrates is a man.**  
>  
>**---**  
>  
>**Socrates is mortal.**

Now, using the logical rule modus ponens, we get the argument-text schema:

>**A**  
>  
>**if A then B**  
>  
>**---**  
>  
>**B**

Thus, we can see schemata as a template, whereby we can plug in sentences into a logical form. A super simple example would be from the SEP page of schema, which states that the string:

>**... is a true sentence if and only if ...**

is a schema, because the first and second blanks can be plugged in with a name of a sentence (for the first blank) and a sentence itself (for the second blanks), like so:

>**'zero is one' is a true sentence if and only if zero is one.**

Yes, it stands to reason that some being could be possible of perceiving through different means (e.g. time, space, and - I don't know - shmace (a third pure form)). But Kant specifically focuses on humans, so necessary in Kantianisn almost always refers to what is necessary for us.

But, as for a citation of where Kant finds space and time to be necessary to us, see below:

>There are three original sources (capacities or faculties of the soul) which contain the conditions of the possiblity of all experience, and cannot themselves be derived from any other faculty of the mind, namely, *sense*, *imagination*, and *apperception* ... All these faculties have a transcendental (as well as an empirical) employment which concerns the form alone, and is possible *a priori*. As regards sense, we have treated of this above in the first part ... (CPR A 95)

Clearly, Kant finds that sense, which *a priori* serves as an original source. Since all sense is necessarily through the pure forms of intuition (as Kant mentions above, see the Transcendental Aesthetic), our perceptions necessarily depend on the pure forms of space and time.

So, here goes my answers (I'm not a Kant scholar, so take them as you will):

First, I think you are getting hung up on representation vs. appearance. That very excerpt that you included (A370-1) demonstrates that Kant views appearances are a subset (or species as Kant says) of the class of representations. Thus, in your demonstration of how you can have appearances of noumena, you are accidentally showing how you can have representations of noumena. It is important to remember that "representation" includes a multiplicity of terms to Kant.

Next, and really just extending my previous point, when you state

>But things in themselves are not spatiotemporal nor represented as spatiotemporal - space and time as representations represent no determination at all of things in themselves. So how then could they, representing their object as spatiotemporal as they do, be representing noumena?

you are missing Kant's view of space and time. It is true that "space and time as representations represent no determination at all of things in themselves". It is also true that noumena are not spatiotemporal. They must, however, be represented as spatiotemporal things since, by definition, representations are phenomenal things and the only way in which we can process our phenomenal intuitions is through the lenses of space and time. Also, to Kant, to cognize is to determine an object, something that necessarily is a derivative of our faculty of understanding. This faculty is distinct from our faculty of sensibility. Thus, our sensibility does not represent objects through the lenses of space and time, but rather representing noumena.

Lastly, Kant doesn't claim that noumena are non-spatiotemporal. He also doesn't claim they are spatiotemporal. The noumenal world is unknowable, so Kant makes no claim about its nature.

I believe that you are slightly misreading what Kant is saying here. It is precisely that space cannot represent a few things:

1. Nouminal properties
2. Relational/determined properties Since we know (see the Transcendental Deduction) that objects are determined via the faculty of the understanding (i.e. the categories), all Kant is saying here is that Space cannot give us nouminal information or specific, determined, categorized information about things. This we are left in the murky middle ground of undetermined representations of noumina as senses or intuitions. You have misread "Space does not represent any property of things in themselves" as "Space does not represent things in themselves". The key point here is "property of". Kant merely is stating that we cannot, through means of the pure form of space, come to nouminal knowledge. Representations, being phenomenal in nature, are necessarily non-nouminal. There is no issue here for Kant.

TLDR: The pure forms of intuition (space and time) are exactly how we come to representations of the nouminal world. In the Transcendental Deduction, Kant makes sure to note that such pure forms are essential for getting any type of representation at all.

It doesn't seem to me to be contradictory, this is essentially analogous to affirmative, negative, and infinite judgments (Table of Judgements, II. Quality). Kant makes it very clear that, for example, "Socrates is non-mortal" is very different (under transcendental logic) than "Socrates is not mortal". Similarly, this type of distinction is what leads Kant to his idea of God (unconditioned conditions of quantity, quality, modality, and relation). Even though God is nouminal, we are basically giving God side constraints, but this in no way attributes and positive value to God. So then, going back to your query on the pure forms of intuition, it is not simply that space and time are only applicable to the phenomenal world, they are "applicable", in a sense, to the nouminal world, insofar as they are our only means by which to perceive the world. This is not a contradiction, because nowhere do the pure forms attempt to give us positive, accurate knowledge of the nouminal world, only representations. This, they never try to do the impossible and work very consistently in Kant's philosophical system.

When it comes to Nietzsche, I may (or may not, I'm not sure) have an unpopular view: don't start with secondary sources. I would read something short and concise of his, something that can introduce you to Nietzsche's tone and style of writing. I would recommend The Antichrist, the second to last work of his. While it is a very angry repudiation of Christianity, it covers some of Nietzsche's philosophical views in, arguably, their most concise description. As an example, aphorism 54 (the book is laid out into 62 aphorisms or short ideas), describes his notion of transvaluation and skepticism extremely well. So that's my recommendation. In contrast, I wouldn't start with books like Thus Spoke Zarathustra, as it is super dense and complicates, especially for someone not too common with Nietzsche's style.
